front: Three core reasons to go asynchronous?
back: Decoupling producers from consumers, buffering traffic spikes, and centralised retries.
No immediate result for the caller, eventual consistency, and an extra critical system (the broker) to run.
A queue absorbs bursts so the consumer processes at a steady rate it can handle.
(arrival rate − processing rate) × spike duration. Drain time = backlog ÷ (processing rate − normal arrival rate).
Each message is delivered to exactly one consumer and removed once processed.
Several identical workers read one queue; each message goes to one of them, spreading the work.
The shared downstream (database, rate-limited API). Past its capacity, more workers add contention, not throughput.
Standard: best-effort ordering. FIFO: strict order within a message group.
Each message published to a topic is delivered to every subscriber.

front: Queue message vs pub/sub message, in meaning?
back: Queue: a task ("do this"). Pub/sub: an event ("this happened").
SNS topic with one SQS queue subscribed per service; workers compete on each queue.

front: Which pub/sub systems retain messages for replay?
back: Log-based ones such as Kafka (retention period, 7 days by default). SNS and RabbitMQ forget a message once delivered.
The broker sends messages as they arrive (RabbitMQ consume, Pub/Sub push). Lowest latency; needs flow control.
The consumer asks for batches when ready (Kafka poll, SQS ReceiveMessage). Natural backpressure.
Caps unacknowledged messages pushed to a consumer, so a slow consumer isn't flooded.
ReceiveMessage with WaitTimeSeconds (up to 20) waits server-side for messages instead of returning empty.
